lessons.title: Structural Analysis
lessons.subtitle: Decoding multisyllabic words by word parts

blocks.text:
Structural Analysis

DECODING SKILL 2 · WORD DETECTIVE

Rule: Long, unfamiliar words are often built from smaller, known parts: prefix + root + suffix. Find the parts you know to decode the whole word.

  • Find the root word first — the main meaning.
  • Peel off any prefix at the start.
  • Peel off any suffix at the end.

Example: un·happi·ly = un (not) + happy + ly (in a way) — "not in a happy way."

Structural Analysis Practice

DECODING SKILL 2 · APPLY IT

Directions: Break each word into prefix / root / suffix, then read it aloud.

1. unfinished    2. replaying    3. disrespectful    4. careless

5. reappearance    6. unbelievable    7. disorganized    8. thoughtfully

Break it down: For each word above, write it like this: un + finish + ed = unfinished.

Challenge sentence: Decode, breaking each long word into parts first: "It was unbelievable how thoughtfully she reorganized the disorganized closet."

THE FUTURE OF EDUCATION

HOW TECHNOLOGY IS TRANSFORMING LEARNING · 2026 EDITION
PERSONALIZED LEARNING is the new standard. AI adapts to each student's pace, providing instant feedback and targeted practice. Classrooms are becoming collaborative hubs.

IMMERSIVE REALITY — Virtual and augmented reality transport students to ancient Rome, the ocean floor, or outer space. Lessons are no longer confined to textbooks. Hands-on simulations make abstract concepts tangible.

GLOBAL CLASSROOMS — Students collaborate with peers across continents. Language barriers fade with real-time translation. Education becomes a worldwide conversation.
DATA-DRIVEN DECISIONS — Teachers use dashboards to track progress and intervene early. Gamification keeps students motivated with badges and challenges.
The future is here — embrace it, learn it, shape it.

THE FUTURE OF EDUCATION

HOW TECHNOLOGY IS TRANSFORMING LEARNING · 2026

Education is evolving. Technology is no longer an add-on; it's the backbone of modern learning. From AI tutors to virtual classrooms, the landscape is shifting rapidly.

What does this mean for students? More personalized, engaging, and accessible learning experiences that adapt to individual needs.

cells.text: Tailored instruction, paced to each student
Learning through experience, not just reading

blocks.text: Read each page carefully. The future is built on these ideas.

pages.title: PERSONALIZED LEARNING
pages.subtitle: ADAPTIVE TECHNOLOGY · EACH STUDENT, EACH PACE

blocks.text: PERSONALIZED LEARNING  ADAPTIVE TECHNOLOGY · EACH STUDENT, EACH PACE

What is it? Personalized learning tailors content, pace, and methods to each learner's unique needs.

How it works: AI algorithms analyze student performance, identify gaps, and adjust difficulty in real time. This allows students to master concepts before moving on, reducing frustration and boosting confidence.

Benefits: Higher engagement, better retention, and improved outcomes. Teachers get detailed analytics to intervene early and support struggling students.
Personalization is not a luxury—it's a necessity.
IMMERSIVE REALITY  VR · AR · LEARNING WITHOUT WALLS

Virtual Reality (VR) immerses students in fully simulated environments. They can explore ancient ruins, dive into the ocean, or walk on Mars—all without leaving the classroom.

Augmented Reality (AR) overlays digital content onto the real world. Point a tablet at a textbook and watch a 3D heart beat or a volcano erupt.

Why it works: Experiential learning boosts memory retention dramatically. When students see, hear, and interact, concepts stick.

AI Tutors provide 24/7 support, answering questions and offering hints. They adapt to each learner's style and pace.

Learning Analytics track progress, identify patterns, and predict outcomes. Teachers receive dashboards with actionable insights.

Early Intervention — when a student struggles, the system flags it instantly, allowing timely support before gaps widen.

GLOBAL CLASSROOMS  BORDERLESS LEARNING · CULTURAL EXCHANGE

Connected Classrooms — students from different countries collaborate on projects via video calls and shared platforms.

Cultural Exchange — learners gain global perspectives, understanding diverse traditions and viewpoints.

Language Skills — real-time translation tools break language barriers, allowing seamless communication.
One world, one classroom.
CONCLUSION  EMBRACE THE FUTURE · SHAPE TOMORROW

The future of education is not a distant dream. It's already here, woven into classrooms worldwide.

Technology empowers learners to explore, create, and connect beyond traditional boundaries.

But the heart remains the teacher. Human guidance, empathy, and inspiration turn tools into transformation.

As we embrace these innovations, we must remember: the goal is not to replace teachers, but to amplify their impact.
The future is bright. Let's build it together.

READING HORIZONS

THE FIVE PHONETIC SKILLS & TWO DECODING SKILLS

WHY IT WORKS: Reading Horizons uses a multimodal approach based on Orton-Gillingham principles[citation:5].

THE METHOD: Direct, explicit, systematic, and cumulative phonics instruction[citation:8].

THE GOAL: Students decode and encode words of any length with fluency[citation:3].

THE FRAMEWORK OF ENGLISH

These 7 skills create a foundation so students master more advanced reading, vocabulary, spelling, grammar, fluency, and comprehension[citation:1].
PHONETIC SKILL 1  ONE CONSONANT FOLLOWS THE VOWEL

THE RULE: When one consonant and nothing more follows the vowel, the vowel will be short[citation:2].

EXAMPLES: sun (s-u-n), cat (c-a-t), mop (m-o-p)[citation:2].

WHY IT MATTERS: This is the foundation of CVC words—the first word pattern students learn[citation:12].

TRY IT: Read these words: sun, cat, mop, dog, hat, top

Say each word aloud. Hear the short vowel sound!
PHONETIC SKILL 2  TWO CONSONANTS FOLLOW THE VOWEL

THE RULE: When the vowel is followed by two consonants and nothing more, the vowel will be short[citation:2].

EXAMPLES: jump (j-u-m-p), last (l-a-s-t), mint (m-i-n-t)[citation:2].

WHY IT MATTERS: This helps students decode CVCC and CCVC words, building on Skill 1[citation:12].

TRY IT: Read these words: jump, last, mint, hand, fast

Notice the two consonants after the vowel!
PHONETIC SKILL 3  VOWEL STANDS ALONE

THE RULE: When a vowel stands alone, it will be long[citation:2].

EXAMPLES: go (g-o), I (I), she (sh-e)[citation:2].

WHY IT MATTERS: This introduces open syllables—a key concept for multisyllabic words[citation:12].

TRY IT: Read these words: go, me, she, we, hi

Hear the long vowel sound at the end!

pages.title: PHONETIC SKILL 4
pages.subtitle: SILENT E MAKES FIRST VOWEL LONG

blocks.text: PHONETIC SKILL 4  SILENT E MAKES FIRST VOWEL LONG

THE RULE: When a word ends with a silent e, the first vowel will be long[citation:2].

EXAMPLES: hope (h-o-p-e), bake (b-a-k-e), tune (t-u-n-e)[citation:2].

WHY IT MATTERS: This is the VCe pattern—a critical long vowel pattern[citation:12].

TRY IT: Read these words: hope, bake, tune, ride, cake

The silent e makes the first vowel say its name!
PHONETIC SKILL 5  ADJACENT VOWELS

THE RULE: When vowels are adjacent, the second vowel is silent, and the first vowel is long[citation:2].

EXAMPLES: boat (b-o-a-t), seat (s-e-a-t), feel (f-e-e-l)[citation:2].

WHY IT MATTERS: This covers vowel teams like ai, ea, ee, oa, and more[citation:10].

TRY IT: Read these words: boat, seat, feel, road, team

The second vowel is silent—the first says its name!
DECODING SKILL 1  ONE GUARDIAN CONSONANT

THE RULE: If there is only one guardian consonant following the vowel, that consonant will move on to the next syllable[citation:3].

EXAMPLES: motel (mo·tel), program (pro·gram), locate (lo·cate)[citation:7][citation:9].

WHY IT MATTERS: This helps students break multisyllabic words into decodable chunks[citation:3].

TRY IT: Break these words: motel, program, locate

The guardian consonant moves to the next syllable!
DECODING SKILL 2  TWO GUARDIAN CONSONANTS SPLIT

THE RULE: When a vowel is followed by two guardian consonants, the consonants will split. The first consonant stays in the first syllable, and the second consonant moves to the next syllable[citation:3].

EXAMPLES: campus (cam·pus), extreme (ex·treme), explain (ex·plain)[citation:9].

WHY IT MATTERS: This is the VC/CV pattern—essential for decoding longer words[citation:3].

TRY IT: Break these words: campus, extreme, explain

The first consonant stays, the second moves on!

READING HORIZONS

COMPLETE PHONICS & DECODING HANDBOOK

WHY THIS HANDBOOK? This book covers the core of Reading Horizons methodology: explicit, systematic phonics instruction.

WHAT IS INCLUDED: The 5 Phonetic Skills, 2 Decoding Skills, Special Vowel Combinations, Blends, Suffixes, and more.

WHO IS IT FOR? Teachers, tutors, and students in grades 2–5 who need a structured approach to reading.

A COMPLETE, SYSTEMATIC APPROACH

Master every rule, practice every pattern, and read every word with confidence.
Table of Contents  WHAT'S INSIDE
Every page is packed with rules, examples, and practice.
PHONETIC SKILL 1  ONE CONSONANT AFTER THE VOWEL

THE RULE: When one consonant follows a vowel, the vowel will be short.

EXAMPLES: sun (s-u-n), cat (c-a-t), mop (m-o-p).

PATTERN: CVC (consonant-vowel-consonant) words.

READ ALOUD: sun, cat, mop, pen, hot, pig

Sound each word aloud and hear the short vowel.
PHONETIC SKILL 2  TWO CONSONANTS AFTER THE VOWEL

THE RULE: When two consonants follow a vowel, the vowel will be short.

EXAMPLES: jump (j-u-m-p), last (l-a-s-t), mint (m-i-n-t).

PATTERN: CVCC or CCVC words.

READ ALOUD: jump, last, mint, hand, fast

Notice the two consonants after the vowel.
PHONETIC SKILL 3  VOWEL STANDS ALONE

THE RULE: When a vowel stands alone, it will be long.

EXAMPLES: go (g-o), I (I), she (sh-e).

PATTERN: Open syllables.

READ ALOUD: go, me, she, we, hi

Hear the long vowel sound at the end.

pages.title: PHONETIC SKILL 4
pages.subtitle: SILENT E MAKES FIRST VOWEL LONG

blocks.text: PHONETIC SKILL 4  SILENT E

THE RULE: When a word ends with a silent e, the first vowel will be long.

EXAMPLES: hope (h-o-p-e), bake (b-a-k-e), tune (t-u-n-e).

PATTERN: VCe (Vowel-Consonant-silent e).

READ ALOUD: hope, bake, tune, ride, cake

The silent e makes the first vowel say its name.
PHONETIC SKILL 5  ADJACENT VOWELS

THE RULE: When two vowels are adjacent, the second vowel is silent, and the first vowel is long.

EXAMPLES: boat (b-o-a-t), seat (s-e-a-t), feel (f-e-e-l).

PATTERN: Vowel teams (ai, ea, ee, oa).

READ ALOUD: boat, seat, feel, road, team

The second vowel is silent—the first says its name.
DECODING SKILL 1  ONE GUARDIAN CONSONANT

THE RULE: If there is only one guardian consonant following the vowel, that consonant moves to the next syllable.

EXAMPLES: motel (mo·tel), program (pro·gram), locate (lo·cate).

WHY: Helps break multisyllabic words into decodable chunks.

TRY IT: Break these words: motel, program, locate

The guardian consonant moves to the next syllable.
DECODING SKILL 2  TWO GUARDIAN CONSONANTS SPLIT

THE RULE: When two consonants follow a vowel, they split — first stays, second moves on.

EXAMPLES: campus (cam·pus), extreme (ex·treme), explain (ex·plain).

PATTERN: VC/CV split.

TRY IT: Break these words: campus, extreme, explain

The first consonant stays, the second moves on.
SPECIAL VOWEL COMBINATIONS  -NG, -NK, -LL

THE PATTERNS: These endings change vowel sounds.

-ng: ang, ing, ong, ung — hang, sing, long, lung

-nk: ank, ink, onk, unk — bank, pink, honk, dunk

-ll: all, ell, ill, oll, ull — ball, bell, hill, doll, pull

READ ALOUD: sing, long, pink, honk, ball, bell

Notice the special vowel sounds.
BLENDS  2-LETTER, 3-LETTER, & EXTRA

WHAT IS A BLEND? Two or three consonants together, each saying its own sound.

2-LETTER BLENDS: bl, cl, fl, gl, pl, sl, br, cr, dr, fr, gr, pr, tr, sc, sk, sm, sn, sp, st, sw

3-LETTER BLENDS: scr, spr, squ, spl, str

cells.text: blip · clam · flag · glad · plug · slip
brag · crab · drip · frog · grab · trip
scat · skip · snug · spot · stop · swim

blocks.text:
READ ALOUD: stop, clap, trip, swim, spot

Hear each consonant sound blended together.
ADDING SUFFIXES  -ING, -ED, -ER, -EST

RULE 1 (Skill 3): If base word ends with a vowel, just add suffix: go → going

RULE 2 (Skill 4): Drop final silent e before adding suffix: hope → hoping

RULE 3 (Skill 5): If base word ends with a vowel team, just add: clean → cleaning

cells.text: go → going · hope → hoping · clean → cleaning
play → played · bake → baked · stay → stayed

blocks.text:
READ ALOUD: going, hoping, cleaning, played, faster

Apply the rule before adding the suffix.
OTHER SOUNDS FOR C & G  SOFT C AND G

SOFT C: When c is followed by e, i, or y, it says /s/: cent, city, cycle

SOFT G: When g is followed by e, i, or y, it says /j/: gem, giant, gym

EXCEPTION: hard c/g usually before a, o, u: cat, go, cup

READ ALOUD: cent, city, cycle, gem, giant, gym

Remember: e, i, y makes c and g soft.
LONG & SHORT VOWELS  REVIEW & IDENTIFICATION

SHORT VOWELS: a, e, i, o, u — as in cat, bed, pig, hot, cup

LONG VOWELS: a, e, i, o, u — as in cake, tree, bike, boat, cube

HOW TO KNOW: Use the Phonetic Skills to determine which sound a vowel makes.

READ ALOUD: cat, cake, pig, bike, hot, boat

Compare short and long vowel sounds.
IDENTIFICATION OF VOWELS  IN WORDS & THREE-LETTER WORDS

VOWELS: a, e, i, o, u (and sometimes y)

HOW TO IDENTIFY: Circle the vowels in each word. Then say the word aloud.

THREE-LETTER WORDS: CVC pattern: cat, dog, sun, pen, pig

READ ALOUD: cat, pig, dog, sun, pen, map

Circle the vowel in each word.
HIGH-FREQUENCY WORDS  READ & SPELL

STEP 8: Introduce a few high-frequency words necessary to read most sentences.

WHY: These words appear often in text and may not follow phonics rules.

HOW: Teach them as sight words—read, spell, and use in sentences.

READ ALOUD: the, of, and, to, in, said, was, are, they, have

Practice these words every day.

READ ALOUD: jump, last, mint, hand, bank

Two consonants make the vowel short.
PHONETIC SKILL 3  VOWEL STANDS ALONE

THE RULE: When a vowel stands alone, it is long.

EXAMPLES: go (g-o), I, she (sh-e).

PATTERN: Open syllable.

READ ALOUD: go, me, she, we, hi

The vowel says its name.
PHONETIC SKILL 4  SILENT E

THE RULE: When a word ends with silent e, the first vowel is long.

EXAMPLES: hope (h-o-p-e), bake (b-a-k-e), tune (t-u-n-e).

PATTERN: VCe (Vowel-Consonant-e).

READ ALOUD: hope, bake, tune, ride

Silent e makes the vowel say its name.
PHONETIC SKILL 5  ADJACENT VOWELS

THE RULE: When two vowels are adjacent, the second is silent, first is long.

EXAMPLES: boat (b-o-a-t), seat (s-e-a-t), feel (f-e-e-l).

PATTERN: Vowel teams (ai, ea, ee, oa).

READ ALOUD: boat, seat, feel, road, team

Second vowel is silent—first says its name.
DECODING SKILL 1  ONE GUARDIAN CONSONANT

THE RULE: If only one guardian consonant follows the vowel, it moves to the next syllable.

EXAMPLES: motel (mo·tel), program (pro·gram), locate (lo·cate).

WHY: Breaks multisyllabic words into decodable chunks.

TRY IT: Break these: motel, program, locate

Guardian consonant moves to next syllable.
DECODING SKILL 2  TWO GUARDIAN CONSONANTS SPLIT

THE RULE: Two consonants follow a vowel: they split. First stays, second moves on.

EXAMPLES: campus (cam·pus), extreme (ex·treme), explain (ex·plain).

PATTERN: VC/CV.

TRY IT: Break these: campus, extreme, explain

First consonant stays, second moves.
SPECIAL VOWEL COMBINATIONS  -NG, -NK, -LL, -LE

-ng: ang, ing, ong, ung — hang, sing, long, lung

-nk: ank, ink, onk, unk — bank, pink, honk, dunk

-ll: all, ell, ill, oll, ull — ball, bell, hill, doll, pull

-le: final syllable — apple, table, little

READ ALOUD: sing, long, pink, honk, ball, apple

Notice the special vowel sound.
BLENDS  2-LETTER, 3-LETTER, & EXTRA

WHAT ARE BLENDS? Two or three consonants together, each saying its own sound.

2-LETTER: bl, cl, fl, gl, pl, sl, br, cr, dr, fr, gr, pr, tr, sc, sk, sm, sn, sp, st, sw

3-LETTER: scr, spr, squ, spl, str

cells.text: blip · clam · flag · brag · crab · trip
scat · skip · snug · stop · spr · str

blocks.text:
READ ALOUD: stop, clap, trip, swim, spot

Hear each consonant sound blended.
ADDING SUFFIXES  -ING, -ED, -ER, -EST

RULE 1 (Skill 3): If base ends with vowel, just add: go → going

RULE 2 (Skill 4): Drop silent e before suffix: hope → hoping

RULE 3 (Skill 5): Vowel team base, just add: clean → cleaning

READ ALOUD: going, hoping, cleaning, played, faster

Apply the rule before adding.
MORE SUFFIXES  -TION, -SION, -TIAL, -CIAL, -TURE, -SURE

-tion: action, motion, nation

-sion: vision, division, decision

-tial / -cial: partial, facial, special

-ture / -sure: picture, nature, measure

READ ALOUD: action, vision, partial, picture

These suffixes change the word's meaning.

pages.title: SOFT C & G
pages.subtitle: OTHER SOUNDS FOR C AND G

blocks.text: SOFT C & G  OTHER SOUNDS FOR C AND G

SOFT C: When c is followed by e, i, y → /s/ (cent, city, cycle)

SOFT G: When g is followed by e, i, y → /j/ (gem, giant, gym)

HARD C/G: Before a, o, u → /k/ and /g/ (cat, go, cup)

READ ALOUD: cent, city, cycle, gem, giant, gym

e, i, y makes c and g soft.
DIPHTHONGS  OI/OY, OU/OW, AU/AW

oi/oy: coin, boy — gliding vowel sound

ou/ow: house, cow

au/aw: haul, paw

READ ALOUD: coin, boy, house, cow, haul, paw

Vowels glide together.
SPECIAL LONG VOWEL COMBINATIONS  OLD, OST, ILD, IND

THE PATTERN: When a vowel is followed by -ld or -st, it can be long.

EXAMPLES: old (long o), most (long o), wild (long i), kind (long i)

WHY: This is an exception to the short vowel rule.

READ ALOUD: old, cold, most, wild, child, kind

This is a special exception.
FINAL -LE WORDS  CONSONANT + LE

THE PATTERN: Words ending in -le form a separate syllable.

EXAMPLES: table (ta·ble), apple (ap·ple), little (lit·tle)

HOW TO PRONOUNCE: The -le sounds like "ul".

READ ALOUD: table, apple, little, candle

The -le forms its own syllable.
HIGH-FREQUENCY WORDS  READ & SPELL

WHAT ARE THEY? Words that appear often in text and may not follow phonics rules.

HOW TO LEARN: Read, spell, and use in sentences daily.

READ ALOUD: the, of, and, to, in, said, was, are, they, have

Practice these every day.

blocks.text: VOWEL REVIEW  SHORT & LONG SOUNDS

SHORT VOWELS: a, e, i, o, u — as in cat, bed, pig, hot, cup

LONG VOWELS: a, e, i, o, u — as in cake, tree, bike, boat, cube

VOWEL Y: Y acts as a vowel at the end of words — fly, baby, gym

READ ALOUD: cat, cake, bed, tree, pig, bike, hot, boat, cup, cube

Notice the difference between short and long vowel sounds.
FINAL PATTERN -ZE  AS IN FREEZE

THE PATTERN: Words ending in -ze have a long vowel sound before the final z.

EXAMPLES: freeze (long e), breeze (long e), sneeze (long e)

WHY: The silent e makes the vowel long.

READ ALOUD: freeze, breeze, sneeze, blaze, doze

The silent e keeps the vowel long.
FINAL PATTERN -AGE  AS IN MESSAGE

THE PATTERN: Words ending in -age usually have a schwa sound (/j/) at the end.

EXAMPLES: message (mes·sage), village (vil·lage), package (pack·age)

WHY: The -age ending is common in nouns.

READ ALOUD: message, village, package, courage, garage

The -age ending sounds like "ij".
DIPHTHONGS  OI/OY, OU/OW, AU/AW

WHAT IS A DIPHTHONG? Two vowels that glide together to form one sound.

oi/oy: coin, boy — mouth glides

ou/ow: house, cow — mouth glides

au/aw: haul, paw — mouth glides

READ ALOUD: coin, boy, house, cow, haul, paw

Vowels glide together to make one sound.
SUFFIXES -TION / -SION  AS IN ACTION & VISION

-tion: action, motion, nation, station

-sion: vision, division, decision, confusion

HOW TO REMEMBER: -tion is more common; -sion is used after certain roots.

READ ALOUD: action, vision, nation, division, decision

These suffixes turn verbs into nouns.
SILENT LETTERS  KN, WR, MB, GH

kn: silent k — knee, know, knife

wr: silent w — write, wrist, wrap

mb: silent b — comb, thumb, climb

gh: silent gh — light, night, high

READ ALOUD: knee, know, write, wrist, comb, light

Remember: one letter stays silent.
SOFT C & G REVIEW  CENT, CITY, GIANT, GYM

SOFT C: When c is followed by e, i, y → /s/ (cent, city, cycle)

SOFT G: When g is followed by e, i, y → /j/ (giant, gym, gem)

HARD C/G: Before a, o, u → /k/ and /g/ (cat, go, cup)

READ ALOUD: cent, city, cycle, giant, gym, gem

e, i, y makes c and g soft.
HIGH-FREQUENCY WORDS  READ & SPELL

WHAT ARE THEY? Words that appear often in text and may not follow phonics rules.

HOW TO LEARN: Read, spell, and use in sentences daily.

READ ALOUD: the, of, and, to, in, said, were, they, have

Practice these every day.
